title: Frames
shortDefinition: A frame is a bone structure (forearm, shin, knee, bicep) connected to the torso to maintain space, not arm strength to push.
whyItMatters: Good frames let you breathe, rotate your hips, and pummel back inside. Bad frames make you defend with straight arms, easy to smash or submit.
deepExplanation:
There are 4 main frame types, each for different situations:

1. Forearm frame (bicep-to-chest), strongest, maintains distance from shoulder. Use in Side Control, Mount escape, Guard retention.
2. Elbow frame (elbow-to-hip), shorter, allows hip rotation. Use when you need to shrimp or bridge.
3. Shin frame, use in knee shield, Half Guard, blocking bodylock or chest-to-chest.
4. Bicep frame (bent arm across chest), short and strong, use when flattened or under direct pressure.

A frame is not a static barrier. It needs active connection, if the elbow slips from shoulder or hip, the opponent inserts chest and the frame dies. A live frame knows when to push, when to rotate, and when to convert to pummeling.
beginnerView:
Three frame rules:
1. Elbow touches hip or sternum, not floating in the air.
2. Do not round your back, straight spine transmits force through bone.
3. When framing, rotate your hips at the same time, a frame does not push, it redirects.

If your arms burn after 10 seconds of framing, you are using muscle instead of bone.
advancedView: Frame is the first phase of a 3-step defensive chain: frame → pummel → attack. A good frame does not last long, it creates enough space to pummel back inside. When they push into your frame, use that force to shrimp out or rotate. Read frames: if their elbow is away from the hip, they are weak; if their elbow is glued to the ribs, they are strong. Transition from frame to wedge (knee) when they commit weight, if they drive in, your knee enters; if they back off, you pummel.
